newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Creditors seen seeking control of S.Korea's Jinro.
newsitem.headline: Creditors seen seeking control of S.Korea's Jinro.

text.p: Creditor banks of South Korea's troubled Jinro Group said on Wednesday they had sought promises from its chairman and his family to give up their share ownership in group companies in return for a rescue package.
Banking analysts said this would give the creditors control of Jinro, the nation's 19th largest conglomerate.

Officials from the Commercial Bank of Korea and SEOULBANK said they planned to ask for a written promise from the group to allow creditors to sell off shares held by chairman Chang Jin-ho's family whenever necessary.
"This is aimed at pressing Jinro to fulfil its earlier pledge to sell its real estate to generate more cash," said Cho Sung-kwon, spokesman at the Commercial Bank of Korea.
Jinro announced last week it would liquidate unprofitable business lines and other real estate to mobilise 1.2 trillion won by 1998 because of financial pressure.

The Jinro group, which has 22 affiliates under its wing, is groaning under debts of 3.2 trillion won used to fund ambitious expansion. Its 74-year-old flagship, Jinro Ltd, is the largest producer of the Korean distrilled spirits "soju".
Creditors said they did not want Jinro to collapse but they wanted the family's shares as collateral in return for a plan to bail it out.
Last week, financial institutions agreed to help support firms suffering from short-term cashflow problems and decided to alllow six units of the Jinro group to suspend paying back debts.
"It is our basic principle to make every effort to prevent defaults by Jinro, given its negative impact on the economy," said Cho at the Commerical Bank of Korea.
South Korean financial markets have been rocked by the collapse of two steelmakers this year under crushing debts -- Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March.

In a move to prevent such a shock, the finance ministry said on Wednesday it sought special legislation to set up a $1.6 billion fund to clean up the mountain of bad debt burdening financial institutions.
Creditors said they planned to extend fresh loans to Jinro once the chairman's family accepted their proposal.
"We just need something concrete to force Jinro to implement necessary steps to push its business back to normal. With a verbal promise, we cannot extend fresh loans," a SEOULBANK official said.

Jinro spokesman Chun Young-tae said the group had not received any official request from the creditors and declined to comment on their plan. Creditors are due to meet on Monday to discuss Jinro's financial problems.
Analysts said Jinro was expected to try to avoid accepting the loans-for-shares proposal.

"If Chairman Chang gives a written promise to give up his shareholdings, it means the management rights will be tranferred to the creditors," said Lee In-hyung, senior economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
"I expect a tug-of-war between creditors and Jinro over the issue," said Yoo Choon-hwan, senior economist at Shinhan Research Institute, a unit of Shinhan Bank.
Analysts said it was too early for the creditors to look for a buyer of Jinro. "I don't think a third-party takeover will be necessary," Yoo said.
